title: Complex Matrix and Grid Puzzles
tagline: Year 3 — Several people, several attributes: elimination grids, linked clues and cross-referencing

introduction.overview: A matrix puzzle assigns several attributes (profession, city, hobby) to a set of people, with one value of each attribute per person. A grid with people down one side and values across the top lets you cross out impossible cells and fill in forced ones. The technique is to record every clue in the grid, look for rows and columns with only one cell left, and use linked clues ("the doctor lives in Pune") to merge attributes into bundles.
introduction.placementRelevance: Grid puzzles with 4–5 people and 2–3 attributes are the standard "hard" puzzle in company reasoning tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Matching customers to products, tasks to people and rooms to guests uses the same elimination logic.

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: In a one-to-one matching, each value belongs to exactly one person. A tick in one cell means crosses in the rest of its row and column.

coreDefinitions: Grid: a table of people against attribute values for marking yes and no.
Positive clue: says a person has a value; tick the cell and cross the rest of the row and column.
Negative clue: says a person does not have a value; cross that cell.
Linked clue: ties two values to the same person ("the doctor lives in Pune").
Bundle: values known to belong to the same person, even before the name is known.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every person ends up with exactly one value from each list. Every tick closes a row and a column, so a few clues cascade into the full solution.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Draw one grid per attribute against the people. Enter positive clues first, then negative clues, then merge linked clues into bundles. When a row or column has a single open cell, tick it and repeat.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: One-to-one
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Each value belongs to exactly one person

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Tick closes
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Tick one cell, cross the row and column

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Elimination
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Last cell left in a row is forced

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Test every clue on the final grid

mainNarrative: Four friends Kavya, Lokesh, Meera and Naveen have different professions and live in different cities. The doctor lives in Pune and the lawyer lives in Delhi (bundles). Lokesh lives in Mumbai, Naveen lives in Delhi, Kavya is a teacher, and Meera is not an engineer. Naveen lives in Delhi, so he is the lawyer. Kavya, a teacher, cannot be the doctor, so she is not in Pune; her remaining city is Chennai. Meera is not an engineer, so she is the doctor and lives in Pune. Lokesh is the engineer.

With three attributes, add the hobby grid and the new linked clues: the person who likes cricket lives in Mumbai; the person who likes reading is the lawyer; the person who likes music lives in Pune. These attach hobbies to the bundles: Lokesh (Mumbai) likes cricket, Naveen (lawyer) likes reading, Meera (Pune) likes music, and the leftover hobby, chess, goes to Kavya.
Linked clues are the most powerful because they merge columns. Once "doctor ↔ Pune" and "music ↔ doctor" are known, music, doctor and Pune are one bundle that belongs to a single person.
Negative clues are used last. They never place a person on their own; they only cross out a cell, which helps when two options remain.
For questions, read the finished grid. "In which city does the person who likes reading live?" means find the reader first, then read the city.

deepDiveAspects.title: Bundles speed things up
deepDiveAspects.content: Treat a bundle as a single "super person" until a named clue pins it to one name.

deepDiveAspects.title: Unique solutions
deepDiveAspects.content: A well-formed puzzle has exactly one solution; if you reach two options, a clue has been missed.

solvedExamples.title: Bundles
solvedExamples.question: The doctor lives in Pune, the lawyer lives in Delhi, and Naveen lives in Delhi. What is Naveen's profession?

steps.title: Bundle
steps.explanation: The person in Delhi is the lawyer.

steps.title: Match
steps.explanation: Naveen lives in Delhi, so he is the lawyer.

solvedExamples.title: Elimination
solvedExamples.question: Kavya is a teacher; the doctor lives in Pune; Lokesh lives in Mumbai, Naveen in Delhi. In which city does Kavya live?

steps.title: Pune
steps.explanation: The Pune person is the doctor, but Kavya is a teacher.

solvedExamples.title: Cross-reference
solvedExamples.question: In the finished grid Lokesh likes cricket and lives in Mumbai. In which city does the person who likes cricket live?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Find the person, then the city.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Enter positive clues, cross rows and columns, merge linked clues into bundles, and fill the last open cell in each row.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to cross the row and column

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject any option that conflicts with one grid cell.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write bundles on the side as you find them.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Five-person puzzles carry six or more questions, so complete the grid once.

easy.question:
Four friends Kavya, Lokesh, Meera and Naveen each have a different profession (doctor, engineer, teacher, lawyer) and live in different cities (Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai, Pune). The following facts are known:
1. The doctor lives in Pune.
2. The lawyer lives in Delhi.
3. Lokesh lives in Mumbai.
4. Naveen lives in Delhi.
5. Kavya is a teacher.
6. Meera does not be an engineer.

In which city does Kavya live?
easy.explanation: Working out the grid gives (profession / city): Kavya: teacher / Chennai; Lokesh: engineer / Mumbai; Meera: doctor / Pune; Naveen: lawyer / Delhi. So Kavya's city is Chennai.
